inspections.locator: Theodore Rousseau, The Stylistic Detection of Forgeries: PDF pages7–12, printed247–252; lines310–538
inspections.assessment: Rousseau distinguishes copying familiar mature Vermeer paintings from filling a missing early period that scholars expected to find. He discusses provenance, Bredius endorsement, museum purchase and collaboration accusation followed by the confession to forgery and a one-year sentence. He describes hardened resin and old supports as material deception. His account of interrogating Miedl is retrospective participant evidence for his own investigation, not a contemporaneous transcript of Miedl or van Meegeren. His stylistic judgments are interpretation. Specific pigment claims and all reported dialogue are not verified here.
inspections.sourceQualityRationale: 1968 museum bulletin by the Met European Paintings department head who says he personally interrogated the intermediary after the war. Valuable participant-linked evidence and expert analysis, written over20years later; no blanket independence or contemporaneity claim.

inspections.locator: Anna Tummers,2009 thesis; printed18–21/PDF18–21; lines389–539; especially427–476 and footnotes7–10
inspections.assessment: Tummers traces endorsement and later resistance to reattribution. Van Meegeren denied selling an authentic Old Master and claimed his own authorship, including other accepted paintings. Workshop evidence and an expert committee tested this. The text distinguishes his explanation of manufacture from laboratory findings about a modern binding medium and cites published1949 investigators and reproduced court statements. It supports the substantial payoff: the material used to fake age also proved modern origin. The thesis says he created a painting during the trial broadly; it does not authenticate a dramatic painting scene in a1947 courtroom.
inspections.sourceQualityRationale: University of Amsterdam doctoral scholarship with named author and footnotes to original1949 tests and period reactions. Secondary historical synthesis; quoted period statements and laboratory reports remain indirectly inspected through it, not independently authenticated originals.

inspections.assessment: RKD describes the collaboration investigation following a supposed Vermeer sale to Göring, van Meegeren claiming forgery, and Coremans leading an international expert committee. It explains X-ray versus surface cracking evidence and contrasts between authentic and suspect paintings. Notes identify Coremans1949 and Froentjes/de Wild1949 original investigations. The evidence was a committee investigation, not one painting performance magically proving innocence.
inspections.sourceQualityRationale: Netherlands Institute for Art History technical history with specific original laboratory-report citations; authoritative domain-appropriate secondary evidence. The original reports are located but not fully inspected; no claim that reproductions on this page are freely licensed production assets.
